newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr learns to live with new heights.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr learns to live with new heights.

text.p: The Australian dollar took a tiny step back Monday as its recent meteoric ascent left some in the market with a touch of vertigo.

But dealers thought the pullback shallow so far given the currency had shot up over a cent last week and had gained almost six percent in little more than a month. A second finish atop the important US$0.7960 chart level also reinforced the bullish technical background and argued for a re-test of 80 cents this week enroute to US$0.8050, they added.
Any deeper correction should be limited to US$0.7925 and it would take a breach of US$0.7835 to reverse the uptrend.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was making itself at home at US$0.7974/79 having spent the session in a relaxed US$0.7970/7990 range.

This was not far from Friday's two-month closing high of US$0.7988/93 and still well up on that day's early US$0.7930. The speed of the climb had left it overbought on daily charts and a band of tough resistance lay ahead to US$0.8050, so some consolidation would come as no surprise, analysts said.
Nevertheless, they noted the dollar had consistently surprised on the upside for the past month and the market was not so long that a top could be called with any confidence.

Also going its way was the continuing exodus of investor funds out of much of Europe -- a German name had been a noteable buyer on Friday -- and Japan where interest rates were at or close to record lows.

In contrast Australian yields had risen sharply in recent weeks as the Reserve Bank took an upbeat outlook on the econmy and the market all but abandoned thoughts of another easing in official policy.
Spreads over U.S. bonds had widened accordingly and the domestic 10-year bond now offered the highest return of any in the OECD at 7.89 percent.

This widening had stirred Japanese demand for A$ assets, including yen/A$ samurais, which was a complete turnaround from earlier in the year when investors were rushing to redeem A$ bonds to lock-in profits.
Some felt the trickle of funds out of Japan could strengthen once the financial year-end passed on March 31, removing the need for institutions to repatriate funds for windowdressing.

That outlook helped keep the dollar well supported at 98.55/65 yen today after it leapt to a 4-1/2 year closing high of 98.62/72 on Friday from 95.80 this time last week and 93.00 at the end of February.
The broad-based nature of its gains was clearly illustrated by the trade weighted index which was up near a six-year peak at 61.4 today from 60.5 a week ago and a 58.00 low last month.

Domestic econmic data were thin on the ground this week with Q4 housing starts and manufacturing input prices out Tuesday the only official releases of note. A new measure of merchandise imports is due Thursday but this is no longer on a balance of payments basis so bears little relation to the current account.
RBA governor Ian Macfarlane was addressing a swaps and derivatives conference on Thursday morning but no details of his subject were yet available. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
